newsitem.title: USA: Enron, Ore. still wide apart on rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Enron, Ore. still wide apart on rate cut.

text.p: The Oregon Public Utility Commission (OPUC) and Enron Corp are still far apart on an adequate rate cut for customers of Portland General Electric Co, which plans to merge with Enron, an OPUC official said Wednesday.
Tom Riordan, an analyst at the commission, said the parties reached agreement at a special meeting Tuesday on other conditions of the merger, but made no progess on the rate cut issue.
"The companies are going to come back to us with another offer," he added.
The staff of the OPUC has called for a $189.6 million rate cut over four years after a merger, while Enron and Portland General offered $40 to $50 million, he said.
The companies originally estimated merger-related savings at around $3 million a year, but came up with the higher offer after a special hearing before the OPUC earlier this month.
At the special hearing, the three-member board said final approval of the merger hinged on a bigger rate cut.
Riordan said the staff of the OPUC and the companies "agreed to disagree" on how to allocate costs of and revenues from unregulated businesses compared with those from regulated operations.
Enron and Portland General have argued that shareholders rather than ratepayers take the risk for unregulated businesses, such as wholesale power trading, and should reap the bulk of any rewards.
The utility has proposed state legislation that would direct the OPUC to adopt policies ensuring that utility rates do not include costs of or revenues from competitive businesses.

The OPUC analyst said Enron and Portland General must now decide whether to come up with a dollar amount that is acceptable to the commission, or propose a lesser dollar amount on the understanding the OPUC will review the the issue at the utility's next general rate case.
Another meeting was scheduled in Salem, Ore., on March 6.

Separately, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) on Wednesday gave its approval to the merger plan, concluding that the $2.1 billion stock-for-stock deal would not hurt competition in the wholesale electricity market.
A spokesman for Enron noted that the FERC decision related to the wholesale side of the deal, while the OPUC is proceeding independently to review the retail side.
A final decision by the Oregon commission had been expected by mid-March, but the parties say that deadline is unlikely to be met.
